nameStory: The cave spider gets its name from its love of dark, cave-like spaces where it builds its messy cobwebs. While it's perfectly happy in actual caves, this adaptable arachnid has also made itself at home in our basements, crawl spaces, and any other dim, humid spot that reminds it of its ancestral underground haunts. The scientific name 'cellulanus' comes from the Latin word for 'small cell' or chamber, referring to its preference for enclosed spaces.
description: The cave spider is a small, pale brown spider that looks like it's been living in shadows its whole life. These tiny arachnids are typically less than half an inch long including their legs, with a round abdomen and relatively long, delicate legs that give them a somewhat fragile appearance. Their color ranges from light tan to yellowish-brown, often with a translucent quality that makes them appear almost ghostly in dim light. You'll recognize them by their messy, irregular webs that lack the organized beauty of an orb weaver's creation.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates irregular, messy cobwebs that feel sticky and disorganized when accidentally walked into - nothing like the neat spiral webs of garden spiders

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small, delicate build with a rounded abdomen and proportionally long, thin legs that appear almost thread-like

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale brown to yellowish coloration with a somewhat translucent appearance, lacking any bold patterns or stripes

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body typically measures less than a quarter-inch, with legs extending the total size to about half an inch across

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with quick, jerky motions when disturbed and tends to retreat deeper into dark crevices rather than dropping or running

habitat: Cave spiders seek out the darkest, most humid corners of New England's landscape, from natural limestone caves and rock crevices to human-made spaces like basements, crawl spaces, and root cellars. They particularly favor areas with consistent moisture and temperatures, often setting up shop near stone foundations, in woodpiles against buildings, or in the damp corners of garages and sheds. You'll rarely find them in bright or dry locations, as they've adapted to life in perpetual twilight.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as temperatures warm, beginning to build new webs and mate. Look for fresh, irregular webs appearing in dark corners of buildings and outdoor structures.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you're most likely to spot adults in their webs. Females may be carrying egg sacs or tending to newly hatched spiderlings in their messy cobwebs.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active, with some individuals reaching maturity. Webs may become more noticeable as they accumulate dust and debris over the active season.
seasonality.winter: Adults can remain somewhat active in heated basements and protected spaces, though outdoor populations may become dormant or die off, leaving eggs to overwinter.

funFact: Despite being called a 'cave spider,' this species is actually an immigrant that hitchhiked its way from Europe to North America, probably hiding in cargo shipments, and has become so successful at colonizing our basements and cellars that many people assume it's a native species!
confusionNotes: Cave spiders are often confused with common house spiders, but cave spiders are paler, more translucent, and prefer much darker spaces. Remember: if you find it in a well-lit room, it's probably not a cave spider - these guys are true shade-seekers who avoid bright areas like vampires avoid sunlight.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'comb-footed cellar spider' can be confusing because it refers to the tiny bristles on their feet that help them handle their sticky webs, but this feature is too small to see without magnification. Don't worry about looking for the 'combs' - focus on their preference for dark, damp spaces instead.
compareHints: Since this is the only Nesticus species commonly found in New England, compare it to other small cobweb spiders in dark spaces. Cave spiders are paler and more translucent than most cellar spiders, and they're more committed to staying in truly dark areas rather than venturing into moderately lit spaces. Their webs also tend to be smaller and more delicate than those of robust house spiders.
